# How to Use Relax Mode in Midjourney (Beginner-Friendly Guide)

Picture this: it's a quiet Sunday afternoon, you're sketching out a storyboard for a side project, and you've just run out of fast image generations. The creative flow is right there — but the tool tells you to wait, or pay more. That's exactly the kind of moment **Relax mode** is built for.

## What Relax mode actually does

Midjourney (an AI image generation tool — think of it as a smart artist you talk to using text instructions) has two main speeds: **Fast mode** and **Relax mode**. Fast mode pushes your image to the front of the queue and gives it back in seconds. Relax mode lets the AI work on your image in the background, on spare server capacity, so it takes longer, but it doesn't eat into your **credits** (the small unit of monthly computing power you're given with your subscription).

The trade-off is simple: speed for cost. If you're not in a rush, Relax is a great way to keep creating.

## How to switch it on in Discord

Before you start: you'll need a Midjourney account with an active subscription, plus access to Discord (the chat app where Midjourney first launched). Once you're set up:

1. Open any Midjourney channel and type `/settings` in the message box, then press Enter.
2. A pop-up panel will appear. At the top of that panel, you'll see a horizontal row of toggle buttons. This is the **mode row** — it usually shows three pill-shaped buttons labelled **Fast**, **Relax**, and sometimes **Turbo**.
3. Click **Relax**. The button will highlight to show it's selected.
4. Now type your **prompt** (the text description of the image you want — for example, *"a fox reading a book in a cosy library"*) in the message box and press Enter. The bot will reply confirming it's processing in Relax mode.

## How to switch it on in the web app

If you use Midjourney's website instead of Discord:

1. Go to midjourney.com and sign in. Click on any image you've already generated (or start a new one) to open it in the full view.
2. Look just above or below the main **Generate** button. You should see a small text label showing the current mode (for example, "Fast"), usually with a little arrow or dropdown next to it.
3. Click that label and choose **Relax** from the list.
4. Hit **Generate** again. Your next image will be made in Relax mode.

**Can't find the toggle?** Try the right-hand sidebar under "Job actions", or open the three-dot menu (⋮) on your image. If it's still not there, your subscription tier may not include Relax — it typically requires at least a Standard plan or higher.

## When to use which

- **Fast mode**: testing ideas, working on a deadline, showing a client something quickly.
- **Relax mode**: refining approved images, exploring variations, personal projects where time isn't critical.

There's a soft cap on Relax usage during busy periods, so if a job is genuinely urgent, switch back to Fast first.

## What this means for you

- **If you're creating for fun or study**: Relax mode is your friend. You can experiment freely without watching your credits drain. Treat it like sending a piece of writing to a friend for feedback — slower, but still useful.
- **If you create content for work**: Use Fast for client-facing deadlines, then switch to Relax for your own R&D (research and development — basically your experimentation time). It keeps "billable hours" separate from "creative play" in a clean way.
- **If you're brand new to AI image tools**: Don't worry about modes on day one. Start with whatever's on by default, get comfortable writing prompts, and come back to this once you've used up a few generations.

## Wrap-up

Relax mode is a small feature with a useful idea behind it: creative work doesn't always need to be instant. Switch it on when speed doesn't matter, save your fast credits for when it does, and you'll get more value out of your subscription without changing anything about how you prompt.

**Try this today:** open your Midjourney `/settings`, switch to Relax, and re-run your favourite prompt from the last week. Compare the new result to your original — you might find the extra think-time produces something you actually prefer.
